destination.title: He Paid $139,000 Cash. There Was No Mortgage. The Bank Padlocked the Door.

candidate_payload_lines: In April 2011 he sat down with Scott Pelley of Sixty Minutes and explained it without embarrassment, because nobody at DocX had ever told him it was wrong.
On the ninth of January 2010, Charlie Cardoso stood outside a house in Spring Hill, Florida, and cut the padlocks off his own front door.
But nobody caught the mistake, because catching it would have meant reading something.
Anyone in Florida could have walked into that building, asked at the counter, and been shown who owned 9168 Geneva Street.
And in late June 2009 their tenant telephoned in a panic.
And on the fifth of January 2010, Bank of America's people came back and padlocked the house again.
On the twentieth of January 2010 the Cardosos filed suit in federal court in Massachusetts.
In 2010 alone, roughly one point two million American homes completed foreclosure.
And the machine went on producing documents about a house it had never looked at, because the documents were not being produced by anyone who looked at anything.
That is the whole mechanism, and it is thinner than it sounds, because in a foreclosure hearing there is very often nobody in the room to argue back.
So the entire structure rests on a question nobody had thought to ask out loud.
On the tenth of December 2009, in West Palm Beach, Florida, a lawyer named Christopher Immel put that question to a man named Jeffrey Stephan.
Nobody in his unit went into the system to verify that the figures were accurate; they relied, he said, on the attorney network that sent the documents in.
Six months later, on the seventh of June 2010, a Maine lawyer named Thomas Cox deposed him again in a second case, and got the rest of it on the record.
Four years earlier, in 2006, a Florida court had sanctioned the very same company for the very same practice.

Between March 2003 and late 2009, according to the United States Department of Justice, DocX produced more than one million fraudulently signed and notarised mortgage documents and filed them with property recorders' offices across the country.
In 2003 she was a shipping clerk for auto parts when her grandson told her about a job at a company called DocX.
She told CBS she had never been a bank vice president.
era_note: Modern America, 2005-2013. Present-day suburban Florida, county recorder counters, bank branches, low-rise office parks, open-plan signing floors, interstate driving and courthouses are all correct. Nothing in this case predates 2003, so period dressing of any kind reads wrong.

shorts.angle: There was no mortgage on the house, and the bank foreclosed on it twice because six separate people had the chance to read the address and none of them did.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the one house and the six missed chances. It does not open the deposition or the signature factory, which the other two Shorts carry.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: How does a bank produce a sworn court document about a house nobody has ever looked at?
shorts.loop_join: L8 says the deed was in the county's filing cabinet the whole time; L1 returns to what that deed said — cash, and no mortgage.

lines.text: Charlie Cardoso paid a hundred and thirty-nine thousand dollars in cash for a house in Florida. There had never been a mortgage on it.
source_lines: He had paid a hundred and thirty-nine thousand dollars for it, in cash, five years earlier. There had never been a mortgage on it.

lines.text: Bank of America's crews emptied the house in June 2009 and padlocked the doors. The right house was ten doors down.
source_lines: Bank of America's crews had emptied it the previous summer and locked him out
The house they meant to take was across the street, about ten doors down.

lines.text: The tenant told them. The owner told them. The bank's own agent told the bank it was foreclosing on the wrong home.
source_lines: The tenant told them. The owner told them. Their own agent told them.
The real estate agent that Bank of America itself had hired to handle the property contacted the bank to tell it that it was foreclosing on the wrong home.

lines.text: A representative said the bank had made a mistake, and that someone would call back within the hour. Nobody ever called back.
source_lines: She said the bank had made a mistake. She said someone would call him back within the hour.
Nobody ever called him back. Not that day, and not on any day after it.

lines.text: His son drove him thirteen hundred miles from Massachusetts to Florida, because there was no longer any other way to be heard.
source_lines: So on the seventh of January his son put him in a car and drove him from Massachusetts to Florida, thirteen hundred miles, because there was no longer any other way to be heard.

lines.text: He bought a bolt cutter, cut every lock off the doors, and broke in through the back screen door.
source_lines: He drove to a hardware store, bought a bolt cutter, came back and cut every lock off the doors, and then had to break in through the back screen door to get inside.

lines.text: The pipes had frozen. Almost everything they owned was gone — the table saw, two refrigerators, the family photographs. Only the attic was untouched.
source_lines: The pipes had frozen because the water and power had been shut off.

Almost everything they owned was gone: the air compressor, the nail gun, the table saw, the lawnmower, two refrigerators, the gas grill, and the family photographs. The only things left were in the attic, which the crews had apparently not found.

lines.text: Nobody caught the mistake, because catching it would have meant reading something. The deed was in the county's own filing cabinet the entire time.
source_lines: But nobody caught the mistake, because catching it would have meant reading something.
9168 Geneva Street was theirs the entire time, in the county's own filing cabinet, in a document anyone could have walked in and read.

shorts.angle: One man signed ten thousand sworn foreclosure documents a month, and a working month contains about ten thousand minutes.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the deposition and what a sworn statement is supposed to mean. It does not tell the Cardoso house story or reach the Georgia factory and the payouts.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If nobody was reading the affidavits, how many of the houses taken on them were the wrong houses?
shorts.loop_join: L8 lands on the one sentence above his signature that he never read; L1 restates the volume that made reading it impossible.

lines.text: One man was signing ten thousand sworn court documents a month, and he was about to testify that he did not read them.
source_lines: And in those same months, outside Philadelphia, one man was signing ten thousand sworn court documents a month, and he was about to testify, under oath, that he did not read them.

lines.text: To take a house through a court, a bank hands a judge a piece of paper, and the paper has to be sworn.
source_lines: To take a house through a court, a bank has to hand a judge a piece of paper, and the paper has to be sworn.

lines.text: One person swears, on penalty of perjury, that they personally know what the loan is, who holds it and what is owed.
source_lines: So the law lets one person swear, on penalty of perjury, that they have looked at the file: that they personally know what the loan is, who holds it, what is owed and how far behind the borrower has fallen.

lines.text: In December 2009 a lawyer asked Jeffrey Stephan how many documents came to him. A round number of ten thousand a month, he said.
source_lines: On the tenth of December 2009, in West Palm Beach, Florida, a lawyer named Christopher Immel put that question to a man named Jeffrey Stephan.
In a month, Stephan said, my team brings to me approximately, I'd say a round number of ten thousand.

lines.text: A working month, at eight hours a day, contains about ten thousand minutes. He was not asked to do the arithmetic.
source_lines: A working month, at eight hours a day, contains about ten thousand minutes. He was not asked to do the arithmetic and he did not do it.

lines.text: Then the question the whole system rests on: so these documents wouldn't be executed on your own personal knowledge? Right, Stephan said.
source_lines: Then Immel asked the question the whole system rests on.
So these documents wouldn't be actually executed on your own personal knowledge?
Right, Stephan said.

lines.text: Six months later he was deposed again. Four hundred documents a day. Do you read every paragraph before you sign it? No.
source_lines: Four hundred documents a day. Do you read every paragraph of a summary judgment affidavit before you sign it? No.

lines.text: The notaries who certified that he had appeared before them were not present. He never read the sentence directly above his signature.
source_lines: The notaries who certified that Jeffrey Stephan had appeared before them and signed were not, he confirmed, physically present.
What he did not do was read the sentence directly above his signature, the one that said he knew these facts personally.

shorts.angle: A company in a Georgia office park produced more than a million forged mortgage documents, and the people whose homes were taken were paid three hundred dollars.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the factory and the price. It does not tell the Cardoso house story, and it does not run the deposition the second Short is built on.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: How many American families lost a house on a document that was manufactured?
shorts.loop_join: L8 ends on the number nobody ever counted; L1 returns to the one number that was counted — more than a million documents from a single company.

lines.text: Between March 2003 and late 2009, one company in Georgia produced more than a million fraudulently signed and notarised mortgage documents.
source_lines: Between March 2003 and late 2009, according to the United States Department of Justice, DocX produced more than one million fraudulently signed and notarised mortgage documents and filed them with property recorders' offices across the country.

lines.text: One name appears on them more than any other. Linda Green was a real shipping clerk for auto parts, and she did nothing wrong.
source_lines: One name appears on those documents more than any other, and the woman it belongs to did nothing wrong. Linda Green was real.
In 2003 she was a shipping clerk for auto parts when her grandson told her about a job at a company called DocX.

lines.text: She told CBS she had never been a bank vice president. Her name went onto hundreds of thousands of assignments in a dozen hands.
source_lines: She told CBS she had never been a bank vice president.
Her name went onto hundreds of thousands of mortgage assignments in a dozen different hands, and she was never charged with anything, because the hands were not hers.

lines.text: One of those hands belonged to Chris Pendley. The qualification for the job was that you had to hold a pen.
source_lines: One of them belonged to a man named Chris Pendley.
The qualification for the position was that you had to be able to hold a pen.

lines.text: He was paid ten dollars an hour. The floor quota was three hundred and fifty signatures an hour. He estimates four thousand a day.
source_lines: He was paid ten dollars an hour. The floor quota was three hundred and fifty signatures an hour. Pendley estimates he alone did four thousand a day.

lines.text: Every one of those pages was filed with a county recorder, and once a document is recorded it is public truth.
source_lines: Every one of those pages was filed with a county recorder.
Once a document is recorded, it is public truth. The factory was not producing paperwork. It was producing title.

lines.text: In 2013 the Federal Reserve published the payment table. Two million, three hundred and fifty-eight thousand people received three hundred dollars.
source_lines: The Federal Reserve published the payment table on the ninth of April 2013.

Add up every category paid at the bottom rate and you get two million, three hundred and fifty-eight thousand, four hundred and forty-one people — out of three point nine million in the table — who received three hundred dollars.

lines.text: There is no number, anywhere, for how many American foreclosures rested on documents that were manufactured. The country stopped counting before it knew.
source_lines: There is no number, anywhere, for how many American foreclosures rested on documents that were manufactured.
because the country stopped counting before it knew.
